Oregon’s pioneering decriminalization effort for drugs is set to expire on Sunday, making way for a new statute that again treats possession of small quantities of hard substances as a crime. Under HB4002, individuals found with fentanyl, heroin, meth or similar drugs can opt either to face a possession charge or to enter a treatment pathway that involves a behavioral‑health program and a deflection initiative designed to keep them out of court.

***
The statute classifies simple possession as a misdemeanor punishable by up to six months in jail. Its goal is to give police clearer authority to act against drug use in public spaces and to impose tougher penalties on those who sell drugs near parks or other public areas.

***
While the law does not compel counties to establish treatment options, it encourages them to create local diversion programs that steer people toward addiction and mental‑health services. Supporters argue this flexibility lets each region tailor solutions to its resources, whereas critics warn it could produce a confusing and uneven patchwork of rules across the state. Portland police chief Bob Day noted that deflection is only available when a person has no other charges, no warrants, no violent behavior and is medically stable.

***
When an officer believes someone qualifies for deflection, they contact the county’s deflection dispatch line to share basic details, verify eligibility and summon a mobile behavioral‑health outreach team. The team has thirty minutes to arrive on scene; if they cannot meet that deadline, the individual is taken to jail instead.

***
P.P.S. In our country, people of all age enjoy eating while shopping, and sometimes they stick out their tongue in surprise.
